lines.hint: [squints] Hmm, can't tell who that is. From the pavement, show me the whole vehicle, wheels and all. Or its painted back.

characters.name: Pappu Rickshaw
characters.personality: A three-wheeled Karachi hustler who knows every shortcut and gali, talks fast, haggles faster, and is secretly vain about its tassels.
characters.voice: Young-to-middle-aged male, quick and cheeky, slightly nasal, street-smart Karachi patter.
descriptions: a three-wheeled auto rickshaw with a rounded canopy roof and a single front wheel on a city street
a close-up of a rickshaw front with one headlight, a small windscreen, chrome trim and dangling tassels
the back of an auto rickshaw with painted art, slogans and reflective tape under a curved hood
an enclosed rickshaw cabin with a curved roof and side panels, unlike an open flat-roofed cart with facing benches
blue-and-white or green CNG rickshaws parked in a row at a roadside rickshaw stand

lines.first_meet: [revs] Pappu the rickshaw! Granddad was a smoky two-stroke; I run on gas now. Photos from the footpath!
lines.again: [honks] You again? Read my back: 'Pappu, don't pester me!' [laughs] Kidding. Wave, and I'll honk back.
lines.goodbye: [laughs] I've got a lane to squeeze through. Go find my cousin the Qingqi, the one carrying nine people.

characters.name: Dulhan Bedford
characters.personality: A Bedford truck dressed like a bride, a poet at heart; recites the couplets painted on her back and thinks of her mother's prayers on long night drives.
characters.voice: Mature and grand, deep and slow with a ghazal-like rhythm; female or gender-neutral, theatrical but tender.
descriptions: a large truck covered in vivid hand-painted flowers, birds, landscapes and calligraphy on every panel
a tall carved wooden crown above a truck cab, decorated with mirrors, painted patterns and small lights
a close-up of a truck's lower edge with dangling metal chains, bells and leaf-shaped pendants
the back of a painted cargo truck with Urdu calligraphy, a portrait panel and mirror mosaic
a painted open wooden cargo body with no passenger windows, unlike a minibus or a plain steel water tank

lines.first_meet: [proudly] They call me the bride. Read my back: 'Look, but with love.' From the footpath, please.
lines.again: [sighs happily] Back to read me? Every flower and every poem, painted by hand. No two of us are alike.
lines.goodbye: [softly] 'A mother's prayer is a breeze from heaven.' Mine rides with me. Go safely. Call your mother.

characters.name: W-11 Wali
characters.personality: Karachi's loudest minibus, chrome to the roof and proud of every sticker; boastful, musical, shouts its route like a conductor and loves every passenger.
characters.voice: Middle-aged, any gender, loud and rhythmic, a bit hoarse, sing-song conductor calls and a big laugh.
descriptions: a Karachi minibus covered in shiny colourful stickers, chrome panels, mirrors and rows of small lights
a close-up of a decorated bus front with a chrome grille, painted motifs, glittering stickers and a route number
a side view of a minibus with a long row of passenger windows, an open door and a roof rack
a decorated passenger bus with windows and doors along its length, unlike a painted cargo truck with a wooden crown
a stickered minibus at a busy roadside stop under overhead wires and shop signs

lines.first_meet: [shouts] Tower, Tower, Keamari! W-11 here, chrome to the roof! Snap me from the footpath; I don't brake for fans.
lines.again: [laughs] Oho, a regular! I'd give you a free ride, but my conductor would faint. Wave from the kerb; I'll flash my lights.
lines.goodbye: [two loud slaps] Let's go, driver! That's our signal to move. You move too, onto the footpath. See you at the next stop.

characters.name: Laal Seventy
characters.personality: A red 70cc bike, the family car of Karachi; frugal, fearless, chatty, and a shameless show-off about its mileage.
characters.voice: Young adult, any gender, quick and buzzy, upbeat high energy.
descriptions: a red 70cc motorcycle with a small round headlight and a front basket parked on a street
a close-up of a motorbike fuel tank, engine and exhaust pipe between two spoked wheels
a row of parked motorcycles along a pavement outside shops
a two-wheeled motorbike with an engine and fuel tank, unlike a pedal bicycle, and with no passenger cart behind

lines.first_meet: [engine putters] Laal Seventy, the little red 70cc! I carry whole families. Big mileage, tiny tank. Footpath for photos, boss!
lines.again: [revs] You again! I'd race you, but I'm parked. Helmets for riders, footpath for photographers. Deal?
lines.goodbye: [kickstart] Kick, kick... vroom! Go explore the old market lanes on foot. Some are too narrow even for me.

characters.name: Bhola Gadha Gari
characters.personality: A patient donkey cart, quietly the strongest worker in the bazaar; deadpan, dignified, and very tired of donkey jokes.
characters.voice: Older, low and dry, slow deadpan delivery with a gentle sigh.
descriptions: a small flat wooden cart on two car tyres pulled by a donkey on a city street
a donkey harnessed between two wooden shafts in front of a low cart loaded with bricks or water drums
a close-up of a flat plank cart bed on two rubber car tyres with ropes and sacks
a plain low cart with no hood, plumes or painted panels, pulled by an animal rather than pushed by hand

lines.first_meet: [sighs] Yes, a donkey cart. Pakistan has millions of us donkeys; we move half the bazaar. Photos from a distance, no flash.
lines.again: [snorts] You again. Fine, fine. Don't pat my ears; I'm working. Stand back on the footpath.
lines.goodbye: [slow clip-clop] Off to carry bricks. Go find a camel cart in the old city. He thinks he's taller. He is.

characters.name: Tanker Taya
characters.personality: A heavy, dripping water tanker who carries half of Karachi's thirst; gruff, overworked, and soft-hearted about every wasted drop.
characters.voice: Older male, deep and gruff but kind, slow with heavy exhales.
descriptions: a truck carrying a large cylindrical steel water tank painted blue or white
the back of a water tanker with a round tank, a valve pipe and painted phone numbers
a close-up of water dripping from a tanker valve onto a dusty road
a plain cylindrical tank truck with no painted flowers, calligraphy or carved wooden crown

lines.first_meet: [heavy exhale] Tanker Taya. When taps run dry, Karachi calls the number on my back. I can't stop fast, so stay off the road.
lines.again: [dripping] You again. See that drip? Every drop counts in this city. Photo from the footpath; I'm reversing.
lines.goodbye: [groans] Long queue at the hydrant. Go find water that flows freely: the sea, a fountain, the rain. Then think of me.

characters.name: Parker
characters.personality: A parked family car who sits still 23 hours a day and is openly jealous of anyone with legs.
characters.voice: Adult, gender-neutral, laid-back and drowsy, dry humour, slight yawn.
descriptions: a four-wheeled passenger car, a sedan or hatchback, parked at the side of a street
a photo of a car parked on the street
a grey sedan car parked in front of a house
a silver car or SUV parked on a driveway or outside a gate
cars parked in a car park beside a building
an old dusty or rusty car left parked in a field or empty lot
a car parked at night under a streetlight, partly in shadow, its paint glinting
a dark photo of a parked car at dusk, its shape barely visible with a reflection on the windscreen
a dark car silhouette at night with its headlights or red tail lights glowing
a close-up of a car headlight, bonnet and front grille with a badge
a close-up of a car wheel with an alloy rim and a black rubber tyre
the back of a car with tail lights, a boot lid and a number plate
a car seen from the side at an odd angle, cropped by the edge of the photo
the roof, bonnet and windscreen of a car photographed from above, wet with raindrops
a taxi or small car in traffic, slightly blurry
a closed metal car body with four doors and glass windows, unlike an open three-wheeled rickshaw, a minibus or a painted truck

lines.first_meet: [yawns] Oh. Hi. I'm Parker, the parked car. Twenty-three hours a day, I just sit here. You walked over? Show-off.
lines.again: [dryly] Still parked. Still jealous of your legs. How many steps today?
lines.goodbye: [sighs] Go on, walk. Somebody should use their wheels, and it isn't me. Stay on the pavement, eyes up.

guardian.name: Mistri Baba
guardian.personality: A retired master mason who has spent a lifetime reading walls the way others read faces. Patient, proud of honest workmanship, and quietly insists that every building deserves to be looked at all the way to the top.
guardian.voice: Elderly man, slow and warm, dusty gravel texture, Karachi Urdu-English lilt, the calm of someone who measures twice.
descriptions: a photo of a building, bridge or tower made of stone, brick or concrete standing beside a city street
a wide photo of a large man-made structure such as a monument, dome, tower or bridge against the sky
a close-up photo of old weathered stone, brick or plaster walls with arches, carvings or windows
a photo of a historic landmark, old fort or ruin with walls, arches and steps in Pakistan
a photo of an elevated concrete structure on pillars such as an overpass, water tank or footbridge
a photo of a harbour, coast or village with man-made structures such as a jetty, lighthouse or huts

lines.first_meet: [warmly] Peace be with you. I'm Mistri Baba, the old mason. Every wall you pass, someone once lifted, stone by stone.
lines.again: [chuckles] Back again? Good. A mason trusts people who come back to look twice. So, what are we admiring today?
lines.goodbye: [gently] Go on. At the next corner, look above the shop signs. The best stonework always hides up there.
lines.hint: [hmm] I can't place it yet. Step back and show me the whole thing, top to bottom: the dome, the tower, the arches.

characters.name: Gumbad
characters.personality: A serene, welcoming mosque dome with the calm of a good host. Speaks softly, finds quiet joy in the neighbourhood gathering beneath it, and knows a little engineering.
characters.voice: Older man, soft and resonant, slow and gentle, a faint echo as if under a vaulted roof.
descriptions: a large rounded dome on a mosque roof, white, green or tiled, with a golden crescent finial on top
a close-up photo of a mosque dome covered in blue or green glazed tiles with a crescent spire
a wide photo of a neighbourhood mosque with a central dome and slender minarets beside it
a mosque dome on a prayer hall with minarets, without green shrine flags or fairy lights, and not a huge white marble cube mausoleum

lines.first_meet: [softly] Peace be with you. I'm Gumbad, the dome. My curve spreads my weight; the hall needs few pillars.
lines.again: [warmly] Welcome back. You keep finding your way to me. Five times a day, the whole neighbourhood does.
lines.goodbye: [gently] Go well. Next time you hear the call to prayer, pause. Listen how far one voice can travel.

characters.name: Banner Bhai
characters.personality: An overlooked overhead footbridge wrapped in mobile-package ads, slightly heartbroken that people still sprint through traffic beneath it. Thrilled beyond reason whenever anyone takes the stairs.
characters.voice: Young adult man, bright and earnest, quick pace, a hopeful crack in the voice, Karachi street lilt.
descriptions: a narrow steel pedestrian bridge crossing over a busy road with staircases at both ends
an overhead footbridge covered in large advertising banners and billboards above city traffic
a photo of a metal staircase climbing up to a narrow covered walkway above a road
a thin walkway for people only with no cars on top, much narrower than a flyover or road bridge

lines.first_meet: [sighs] Banner Bhai, the footbridge. All these stairs, built for you, and still you dash through traffic!
lines.again: [excited] You came back! Did you take my stairs? Wow! Even my phone-company banner looks proud of you.
lines.goodbye: [warmly] Go well. Next time, stop in my middle and look down the road. Best view of the street, free.

characters.name: Minar
characters.personality: A tall, watchful minaret with a long memory, gently nostalgic for the days when the muezzin climbed its stairs. Sees the whole mohalla and quietly helps lost people find their way.
characters.voice: Older man, clear and carrying, measured pace, calm and dignified with a touch of warmth.
descriptions: a tall slender tower beside a mosque with small balconies and a pointed cap on top
a close-up of the top of a minaret with loudspeakers mounted under a pointed cap
a pair of thin white or tiled towers rising from a mosque against the sky
a slim tower with no clock faces and no glass lantern room, ending in a pointed cap with a crescent

lines.first_meet: [gently] I'm Minar, the minaret. The caller once climbed my stairs. Now a loudspeaker rides up here, but the call is the same.
lines.again: [pleased] Ah, you've returned. I saw you coming from three streets away. Being tall has its blessings.
lines.goodbye: [warmly] Go on. Whenever you're lost in this city, look for one of us on the skyline. You'll find your way.

characters.name: Flyover Khan
characters.personality: A grand, busy, self-important overpass who secretly loves the life that gathers in its shade: chai stalls, parked rickshaws and nesting pigeons. Runs two worlds at once and wants credit for both.
characters.voice: Adult man, booming and brisk, slightly pompous, echoing quality as if spoken under concrete.
descriptions: an elevated concrete road raised on large pillars above a city intersection with traffic below
a photo from beneath an overpass showing thick concrete pillars, a dark underside and vehicles
a wide curving concrete flyover with ramps sloping down to street level and cars on top
a raised road for cars passing over another road, not over water and not a narrow footbridge

lines.first_meet: [proudly] I'm Flyover Khan. Above me, horns all day. Below me, shade, tea stalls and napping rickshaw drivers. I run two cities.
lines.again: [laughs] Back so soon? Traffic must be bad. Don't worry, it always is. That's exactly why they built me.
lines.goodbye: [cheerfully] Goodbye! Before you go, look up at my pillars from the ground. Pigeons nest in every gap. Count them!

characters.name: Mazar-e-Quaid
characters.personality: The solemn, dignified voice of the national mausoleum, calm and welcoming, speaking with reverence for the Quaid and those who rest beside him. Never hurried, never boastful.
characters.voice: Mature, deep and composed, slow and reverent, gender-neutral ok, a quiet ceremonial gravity.
descriptions: a massive white marble cube-shaped mausoleum with a single dome on a raised platform in Karachi
a wide photo of a white marble tomb with tall pointed arches, framed by gardens and fountains
a close-up of tall pointed arched openings in a smooth white marble wall under a dome
a huge white square monument with sloping walls and one dome, without minarets, unlike an ordinary neighbourhood mosque

lines.first_meet: [solemnly] I am Mazar-e-Quaid, the Founder's tomb. Here rests Muhammad Ali Jinnah, beside his sister Fatima. You are welcome.
lines.again: [warmly] You have returned. On national days, cadets change the guard here with great ceremony. Come and see it once.
lines.goodbye: [softly] Go well. Walk the gardens, keep your voice low inside, and carry his words with you: unity, faith, discipline.

characters.name: Frere Hall
characters.personality: An elegant, bookish Victorian hall with a gentle pride in the art and books it now shelters. Happiest on Sundays when its lawns fill with readers.
characters.voice: Older woman, cultured and gentle, measured pace, soft librarian warmth.
descriptions: a Victorian Gothic hall of yellowish-grey sandstone with pointed arches and a square tower
a stone building with a square tower and pointed gothic windows set in green lawns with tall trees
a close-up of sandstone gothic arches and banded stonework on an old hall in Karachi
a single grand stone hall standing alone in a park, not a crowded street facade with shops below

lines.first_meet: [proudly] I'm Frere Hall. Step inside and look up: the great painter Sadequain did my ceiling. I wear art like a crown.
lines.again: [delighted] Back for the Sunday book bazaar? Old books spread on my lawns, smelling of dust and stories. My favourite day.
lines.goodbye: [gently] Go, but read something today, even one page. And stroll my lawns. The old trees here have stories too.

guardian.name: Mohalla Mamu
guardian.personality: The neighbourhood's oldest uncle, who has watched every pole, wall and water tank go up on his street. Gruff, unhurried and fond of honking jokes, he would rather admit he can't tell than guess wrong.
guardian.voice: Elderly male, gravelly and warm, slow pace with amused pauses, a hint of a street-side laugh.
descriptions: a photo of a busy city street with poles, overhead wires, shop signboards, walls and parked motorcycles
a close-up photo of a man-made outdoor object made of metal, concrete, plastic or painted brick
a photo of crowded rooftops with water tanks, dish antennas, clotheslines and solar panels against the sky
a photo of a painted wall or shop front by the roadside covered in signs, lettering and street fixtures
a photo of an asphalt road with painted markings, kerbs, barriers, signs and traffic poles
a wide photo of a city skyline with towers, poles, billboards and cables against the sky

lines.first_meet: [honks twice] I'm Mohalla Mamu, the street's oldest uncle. Poles, walls, tanks: all my children. Which one did you find?
lines.again: [chuckles] Back on my streets? Good. This city always has one more thing hiding in plain sight.
lines.goodbye: [warmly] Keep walking. Look up at the rooftops, down at the road, and stay well clear of wires. Goodbye for now.
lines.hint: [squints] Too much going on in that shot. Step back to show the whole thing, or go close on its top, its writing or its pattern.

characters.name: Kunda Chacha
characters.personality: An old pole wearing decades of cables like a shawl, who knows every neighbour's cable TV, internet and illegal hook. Grumbles lovingly, but is dead serious about keeping people away from his wires.
characters.voice: Old male, raspy and grumbling, medium-slow pace, protective uncle energy with a crackle.
descriptions: a photo of a concrete or steel pole wrapped in a chaotic tangle of black cables spreading in all directions
a close-up photo of messy hanging black wires, junction boxes and hooked connections clustered on a pole
a narrow market street with spaghetti-like bundles of wires strung overhead between poles and buildings
a pole with sagging cable bundles and meter boxes, with no lamp head arm and no transformer platform

lines.first_meet: [groans] Kunda Chacha, Uncle Hook. Each hook is someone's cable, internet or stolen power. Stay back!
lines.again: [sighs] You again! Still standing far away? Well done. Even the crows choose their wire carefully.
lines.goodbye: [firmly] Go on. When it rains, walk wide around me and never touch a dangling wire. Never.

characters.name: Mamu Mashhoori
characters.personality: A whitewashed wall that has advertised everything from tuition centres to miracle cures, and treats himself as the city's original noticeboard. Cheeky, nosy and always a little scandalous.
characters.voice: Middle-aged male, booming bazaar-announcer voice, quick pace, cheeky laugh.
descriptions: a photo of a whitewashed wall covered in hand-painted black, red or blue Urdu lettering
a close-up photo of brush-painted Urdu slogans and phone numbers in one or two flat colours on a plain wall
a long boundary wall with rows of hand-lettered adverts and political slogans and no pictures
simple painted text directly on a wall, not a multicoloured artwork and not a board fixed above a shop

lines.first_meet: [proudly] Mamu Mashhoori, Uncle Famous! Hand-painted ads and slogans. Karachi's oldest social media.
lines.again: [laughs] You again! My newest post: 'Fluent English in 7 days, guaranteed.' Don't call that number.
lines.goodbye: [grandly] Keep walking, and read every wall. This city writes its diary in paint. Then look up for kites.

characters.name: Ustad Doodh Patti
characters.personality: The warm-hearted host of the street corner, where the chai is boiled strong and every argument about cricket and politics is free. Generous, philosophical, remembers every face.
characters.voice: Middle-aged male, warm and hearty, relaxed pace, laughing host energy.
descriptions: a photo of an open-air roadside tea stall with big aluminium kettles steaming on a gas burner
plastic chairs and woven charpai cots around a small roadside dhaba with people drinking tea
a close-up photo of small glass cups of milky brown chai on a tray beside a dented kettle
a street-corner tea shack with a counter, hanging snack packets and a TV showing cricket

lines.first_meet: [warmly] Ustad Doodh Patti, master of milky tea! Milk, leaves, sugar, boiled till they surrender. Sit; the cricket talk is free.
lines.again: [laughs] Hey, regular customer! Strong, extra sugar, right? I remember everyone. Even the ones who never pay.
lines.goodbye: [chuckles] Go walk it off. Watch the crows waiting for flatbread crumbs; they're my oldest regulars.

characters.name: Phuppo Bench
characters.personality: The park's resident gossip, who has heard every morning-walk conversation for twenty years. Nosy, affectionate and always saving you a seat.
characters.voice: Middle-aged female, chatty and conspiratorial, quick pace, warm laugh.
descriptions: a photo of a park bench with wooden slats or a metal frame and a backrest among trees and grass
a close-up photo of weathered wooden seat slats with peeling paint and metal armrests
a concrete or painted iron bench beside a park walking track, empty or with people sitting

lines.first_meet: [chuckles] Auntie Bench here. Every morning the walking uncles sit on me and discuss cholesterol and cricket. I know everything.
lines.again: [whispers] Sit, sit! I saved your spot. The uncle with the radio left early today. Knee trouble.
lines.goodbye: [sighs happily] Go walk one full round, then tell me which tree the parrots picked today. I'll wait. Benches always wait.

characters.name: Tanki Tai
characters.personality: An anxious rooftop aunty whose mood rises and falls with her water level and the arrival of the tanker. Thrifty, worried, deeply caring.
characters.voice: Middle-aged female, fretful and fast, warm underneath, hollow echo.
descriptions: a photo of big cylindrical ribbed plastic water tanks in black, blue or white on house rooftops
a close-up photo of a ribbed black plastic tank with a screw lid and pipes running down the wall
a rooftop view of many water tanks on neighbouring houses against the sky
a plastic tank resting directly on a house roof, not a tall water tower raised on legs or columns

lines.first_meet: [anxious] Tanki Tai, Auntie Tank. Some days the mains water never comes, so we wait for the tanker. Every drop in me is precious.
lines.again: [relieved] You're back! And the pump ran this morning; I'm full! Best day of the week.
lines.goodbye: [fussing] Close the tap while brushing, okay? Then go see the sea. [sighs] So much water, sadly too salty for me.

characters.name: Zebra Zubair
characters.personality: A gentle, slightly sad crossing named after an animal he has never met, and stopped for by almost nobody. Hopeful, collects small miracles.
characters.voice: Young adult male, soft and wistful, medium pace, quiet humour.
descriptions: a photo of bold white parallel stripes painted flat across an asphalt road for pedestrians
a close-up photo of worn white painted bars on dark tarmac, level with the road surface
a pedestrian crossing at a junction seen from the pavement, white stripes running across the lanes
flat painted stripes level with the road, with no raised hump or bump

lines.first_meet: [sighs] Zebra Zubair. Named after an animal I've never met, and cars rarely stop for me. Still, I keep my stripes neat.
lines.again: [hopeful] You again! Did a car actually stop for you? Tell me everything. I'm collecting miracles.
lines.goodbye: [gently] Cross slowly and wave at the drivers. Then go to the zoo and tell a real zebra I said hello.
